**The exemptions hold in both directions**, which is what keeps them
from outliving their reason: a kind named exempt that starts being
probed fails too. Both halves were sabotaged and seen to fail -- a
removed `VARINT` probe fails by kind name, and a probe added for
`RESERVED` fails with *"the drivers now ask about 58 of its 58
members"*.

And a third test says what the partition cannot: `NOTHING`, `OPAQUE`
and `UNPLACED` have no corpus members, so nothing is claimed about them
either way -- asserted, so the day a corpus schema grows one, the
silence is re-measured rather than inherited.

#### The detector could not see the one case that mattered

**The second sabotage passed, and should not have.** `asks` stores an
`Ask.local` through `c_name`, and my coverage walk compared the raw
`traverse.local_name`. For an ordinary identifier the two spellings are
identical, which is why the first sabotage worked; they differ for
exactly the kind being exempted -- `<reserved0>` against `reserved0` --
so a probe for a reserved member was invisible to the test asserting
that none exists.

A count inherits its detector, inside a test written to catch that
shape. The useful part is which sabotage found it: direction one passed
with the bug present, and only the direction that exercised the EXEMPT
kind exposed it. **A guard tested in one direction is tested on the
case it already handles**, which is the argument for sabotaging both
ends of a two-directional claim rather than the end that reads more
naturally.

### 26.639 The differential asked a run of structs nothing at all

26.638 closed a count that answered zero in C and `None` in Python while
the four-way differential called the cell `agreed`. **This is why it
could**: a `Member.VARIABLE` run whose elements are STRUCTS reached no
branch in `differ.asks`. `indexed_elements` is false for it and
`scalar` is None, so neither the run-element probe nor the byte-run
probe fired, and nothing else claimed it. The driver asked that member
no question in any language, and four backends agreeing about a question
nobody put is what `agreed` meant.

**It is not a composed-schema curiosity.** Both of the corpus's
`[remaining]` runs of structs are this shape --
`mqtt.subscribe_body.filters` and `mqtt.unsubscribe_body.filters` -- so
the four walks over MQTT's topic filters had never been compared with
each other either. The construct has been in the corpus since the
differential existed.

The fix is one branch and one probe: a run of structs is asked for its
`count`, which is the question the three other spellings of it already
get -- `RECORD_RUN`, `TLV` and `INDEXED` all ask exactly this, and the
comment above them says why, *every count is a walk over numbers the
message chose*. A struct run sized by the message is the fourth
spelling of the same sentence and was the one left out.

**Checked that the probe is ASKED, not just that the suite is green.**
`differ.asks` now answers `[('scalar', 'n'), ('varint', 'skip'),
('count', 'run')]` for the cell, and `run_count` appears in the C
driver; mqtt's two bodies answer `[('scalar', 'packet_id'), ('count',
'filters')]`. Without that check a green suite would have been the same
vacuous pass the bug lived in -- which is the whole lesson of the entry
above this one, so verifying it was not optional.

And the cell that exposed 26.638 now reports `agreed` with the count
actually compared, which is stronger evidence for that fix than the
three probes I ran by hand: three backends verified by running and one
by reading becomes four compared against each other on drawn bytes.

**And the probe is HELD BACK, which 26.641 records.** The corpus agreed
under it and the composition space did not: the gate found four
backends splitting three ways on a count the message lies about, and a
schema-level test found five members the WALKER cannot count. Both are
obstacles in front of the probe rather than faults in it, and
`HELD_BACK = False` carries them where somebody turning it on will read
them.

**Its first run failed on the right thing too.** It asked
`edges.pieces.two[2]` for a count, and C emits a schema-stated count as
a MACRO rather than an accessor -- so the driver would not compile. The
condition carries `array_count is None` now, which is not a workaround
but the sentence the three probes beside it are written on: *every count
is a walk over numbers the MESSAGE chose*. A count the schema states is
the same constant in four languages by construction and there is
nothing to compare. Both shapes the probe exists for keep it --
mqtt's two bodies and the composed cell all still answer `count`.

#### What this says about the probe list

The differ's docstring has always ended with the honest sentence *"what
is probed is a subset, and the subset is the thing to grow"*, and it
lists what the subset has cost each time it was short: a wide-scalar run
whose count came from the message (26.47), HTTP's status code and
cpio's thirteen hex fields, SMTP's reply code. This is the fourth such
hole and the first one found by a lens rather than by a defect: the
composition sweep produced a cell whose count was wrong in two backends,
and the blind spot was what let it stay wrong.

**So the subset is worth auditing against `traverse.classify` rather
than grown by instalments.** Every `Member` kind either reaches a probe
or is deliberately out, and today that is a reading of a long `elif`
chain rather than a statement anybody can check. A test asserting the
partition -- every kind probed or named as exempt, with the reason --
is the shape this project uses for the builder's refusals, and it would
have found this hole without a defect to point at it. That is the next
piece of work here, and it is not large.

### 26.638 A `remaining` run of fixed elements counted zero, in four backends

26.635 recorded this as a decision for whoever owns the readers. **It is
a bug, and the measurement that says so took ten minutes**: the element
is `SIZE_FIXED 3` with its own `_required`, so the count is
`(limit - offset) / 3` and the two backends that declined to emit it
declined on a reason that is false for a fixed-size element. The
guidelines' *measure the feared cost before deliberating* applied to a
question I had deferred rather than measured, and the measurement
removed the branch instead of informing it.

What each backend did with `rec run[remaining]`, where `rec` is three
fixed bytes:

| C | `return (uint32_t)0u;` -- so `run_at` refused EVERY index |
| Python | `return None` -- `run(0)` raised comparing `int` with it |
| C++ | no accessor, with a stated reason |
| Rust | no accessor, same stated reason |

The reason the last two give is *"one `rec` cannot be measured from its
own bytes, so a run of them can neither be counted nor walked"*. True of
an element with no single size; false of this one.

**The sibling branch had already been fixed for exactly these two
symptoms.** The walking count's own comment records them: *"
`_count_expression` had no answer and returned the fallback zero -- so
the run read as empty... C++ formatted a Python `None` into the same
accessor, which at least did not compile."* That fix was made for
elements with NO single size, and the fixed-size case kept falling
through to `array_count or 0`, which for a `remaining` run is zero. A
rule written under one configuration, met by the second configuration a
year later -- and the first fix's own evidence was sitting next to the
second fault the whole time.

**The fix is one rule rendered four ways**, beside the walk rather than
inside it: a run of one-size elements needs a division, not a walk.
Guarded in each language's idiom, which is worth stating because they
are not the same device -- C tests the base against the limit, Python
clamps with `max(..., 0)`, Rust uses `saturating_sub`, C++ a ternary.
The offset accessors saturate at the view today, so none of the guards
can fire; they are there for the day one of them stops, where an
unsigned wrap answers a very large count rather than zero.

Verified by RUNNING, not by reading, on the same twelve bytes: C,
Python and C++ each count 3, read back `0102 03`, `0405 06`, `0708 09`,
and refuse index 3. Rust is read from its emitted source and left to the
gate's cross-test.

#### Why nothing else had found it

**No corpus schema has the shape.** The corpus's two `remaining` runs of
structs are mqtt's `subscribe_body.filters` and
`unsubscribe_body.filters`, and both have variable-size elements -- so
both take the walking branch, which works. The fixed-element case exists
only in the composition space, which is where 26.635's lens found it.

**And the four-way differential reports the cell as `agreed`**, because
it compares answers to drawn packets and no driver asks for this count.
That is unchanged by this fix: the backends now agree on a right answer
where they agreed on nothing before, and the differential still cannot
see it. **The coverage gap is the open half** -- a driver that asks for
every run's count would have caught this in 2026, and writing one is its
own piece of work.

What is closed is the defect. What is open is that nothing in the
regression net would notice if it came back, apart from the constructed
test this entry's commit adds.

### 26.637 Fold: the sweep command that cannot answer zero, signalled

Two sweeps in this session read as a leak and both were the sweep's own
shell. `running-code.md` prescribes

    ps -o pid,ppid,stat,etime,rss,cmd --ppid 1 | grep -i <name>

after a run, and the pattern is in the command line of the shell doing
the matching -- so a CLEAN sweep, which is the result the sweep exists
to establish, reads back as one.

    ps ... | awk '$3=="funk" && $2==1' | grep -icE "pytest|qemu|make"
                                     counted 1,  alive 0
    ps ... --ppid 1 | grep -iE "pytest|cc1"
                                     counted 2,  alive 0

**The second is why "subtract one" is not the remedy.** It answered TWO
because the eval ran a pipeline whose shell and subshell both carried
the pattern, so the inflation is a function of how many shells the
command happens to spawn. Printing the rows and reading them caught
both.

And 26.634 has the same class pointed at situ's own output rather than
at the process table: `situc build | grep -c "no builder"` printed 0,
which read as "nothing refused" and meant "the pattern does not match a

**Signalled rather than fixed, and the entry is named**: the sweep

### 26.635 The writer over the composition space, and what the readers do there

Every fault these increments found was in a shape the corpus does not
have: a wide run sized by an expression, a nested struct one byte wide, a
packed member counting a run of structs, a member named after one of the
writer's own locals. **So the lens is the composition space**, which
`tool/sweep.py` has enumerated since 26.47 -- 9000 cells of one construct
after another, in six places -- and which nothing had ever pointed at the
writer.

It is cheap to point there. The planner needs no compiler and no
subprocess, so **the whole space is 77 seconds** rather than the hour the
four-backend sweep takes, which is what makes it worth running over 9000
cells instead of a sample.

What it asks is the claim gate's own question, over schemas nobody wrote:
a struct is planned or refused and never neither, the planner does not
raise, and each refusal carries exactly one claim that holds of the
member it names.

**13356 plans, 5544 claimed refusals, no crash, no silent cell, no false
claim, no ambiguous one** -- and, on the first run, **36 refusals with no
claim at all.** All 36 were one message, the one the packed branch gained
in 26.630 for a member that counts a run of structs: the corpus has no
such member, so the row the gate needs had nowhere to come from. It is in
the table now, and the composed sample reaches it twice, which is why it
is listed as exercised rather than exempt.

The sampled gate is 400 cells in the suite, with the whole space behind
`sweep.py --writer`: `test_composed_schemas.py`'s split, for its reason
-- what belongs in a suite is a fixed sample, and the long run is a tool
somebody chooses to start.

#### What the same lens says about the READERS

The compile half of it found eight of 120 sampled cells whose generated
code will not build under `-Wall -Wextra -Werror`, and **every one was in
the reader's header rather than the writer's**: `-Wsign-compare` in a
generated loop bound, and `-Wunused-parameter` on a `view` nothing reads.
The project's own four-way harness compiles with `-std=c11 -O1` and no
warning flags, so nothing had asked.

**And one of those warnings was standing on a defect.** The unused `view`
is in this:

    static inline uint32_t situ_held_run_count(situ_view_t view)
    {
        return (uint32_t)0u;
    }

for `rec run[remaining]` inside a nested struct, where `rec` is three
fixed bytes. The count is not zero; it is what is left of the view
divided by three. `situ_held_run_at` checks `index >= run_count(view)`,
so **every index refuses**: no element of that run is reachable in C.

Python emits the same accessor returning `None`, and indexing it raises
`TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'int' and
'NoneType'`. **C++ and Rust emit neither**, with a comment saying why --
*"one `rec` cannot be measured from its own bytes, so a run of them can
neither be counted nor walked"*.

So four backends take three positions: two refuse with a reason, one
answers zero, one answers None. Both of the answers are verified by
running rather than by reading, with the inner view constructed directly
through `situ_held_view` and `cell.held.at`, which both backends offer.

**The four-way differential reports this cell as `agreed`**, which is the
finding under the finding: it compares the answers four backends give to
drawn packets, and nothing in it asks for this count. A sampled
differential over 24 of 9000 cells could not have found it either way.

~~Which of the three positions is right is a decision rather than a
gap.~~ **It was not a decision and this paragraph was wrong.** Ten
minutes of measurement -- the element is `SIZE_FIXED 3` and has its own
`_required`, so `(limit - offset) / 3` is its count -- made it a bug
with one answer, fixed in all four backends in 26.638. What survives of
the paragraph is its second half: the differential still cannot see the
accessor, so the coverage gap is the part that is open.

### 26.634 A struct argument is the writer's parameter

0050's construct from the writing side, and three refusals said *`block`
comes from a struct argument*. It does, and that is what makes the struct
writable rather than what stops it.

**A `parameter` member is not in the message.** The length it states came
from somewhere else -- a negotiation, a transport header -- and the schema
says so. A reader takes it per accessor,
`situ_negotiated_payload_len(view, arg_block)`; a writer takes it once,
because it puts the whole struct down in one call. So the runs it sizes
have **no `_len` parameter at all**: `payload[block]` is `arg_block`
bytes and `trailer[block + 1]` is one more, which is the FORWARD
direction of the linear form a computed size field inverts. Asking the
caller for those lengths as well would be two numbers for one fact, which
is the rule every size field here follows.

    situ_negotiated_build_marker(out, cap, 3, body, tail, 0xBEEF,
                                 mark, 2, &wrote)
    -> A1A1A1 B2B2B2B2 BEEF 01 C3C3

Three bytes of payload and four of trailer, from one argument of three,
and the reader validates it with the same argument.

**The argument goes first, in member order**, because that is where the
schema declares it and this writer's contract is *one member at a time in
schema order*. The reader puts its arguments last for its own reason: an
accessor takes one view and whichever arguments that member needs. The
NAME is shared -- `traverse.argument_name` now, moved out of
`codegen/c/emit.py` -- because a caller holding one value for both should
not have to learn two spellings of it.

#### Two tools caught what reading did not

**The assertion fired, which is what it is for.** The inversion pass
declined `trailer` for the very fact that makes it writable, so
`_member_refusal` reached a size expression with no reason attached and
asserted. That assertion was added in 26.630 to catch a message composed
from the expression alone; it caught the opposite case a day later.

**And the epilogue called `_validate(view)` where the reader's signature
is `(view, arg_block)`** -- a compile error rather than a quiet one,
which is the direction worth having. A parameter is in no byte, so every
accessor and the validation take it passed.

#### A grep that could not see a traceback

Worth recording against myself. The run that should have shown the
assertion was `situc build ... | grep -c "no builder"`, which printed
`0` -- and I read that as "nothing refused" when it meant "the pattern
did not match a Python traceback". The traceback was on the very next
line of a stream I had filtered.

That is `evidence.md`'s *never reduce a check's output before you know it
passed*, in the one place it is easiest to break: a count over a filtered
stream, in a shell pipeline, where the exit status belongs to `grep`
rather than to the thing being measured.

**180 of 242 structs build**, 36 of 45 schemas, 99 of 112 arms.

#### And one piece of work that measurement cancelled

The next candidate was the scaled text number -- json's `number`, which
0056 calls that schema's largest silence. Two things came out of reading
before writing:

**It needs 0056's open question settled.** That record says in as many
words that *what a canonical decimal spelling is remains open* and is
*not one to settle in the record that introduces the construct*. A writer
must choose a spelling, and for a positive scale the choice is real:
`(1, 3)` is `1e3` keeping the pair and `1000` keeping only the value.
`1e3` is the only one that round-trips the pair, and the pair is
deliberately a reading of the SPELLING -- which is 0056's own argument
against normalizing.

**And it would buy one struct, not json's.** `json.number.value` ends
`before` any of THREE delimiters, and both of those are refusals already
in the table for reasons that have nothing to do with scaling: the byte
that ends it belongs to the object, and which of three to write is not
stated. So a scaled formatter unlocks `edges.measured` alone.

A question that survives measurement is a real decision and goes to
whoever owns it; this one shrank to one corpus struct behind an open
decision, which is a different answer from "hard" and the reason the work
was not started.

### 26.633 A nested struct one byte wide is not a byte run

Three refusals said *`flags` has no stated length, so nothing says when
the writer should stop*. Its length is one byte and fixed.

**The branch asked how wide an element is**, and a byte-wide element is
exactly what a byte RUN has -- so `flags flags;` went down the run path,
found no count there, and reached the fall-through refusal. The three are
`message.header.flags`, `telemetry.reading.status` and
`header.header.flags`, each a group of bits that closes a byte exactly,
which is the commonest shape a protocol header has. A nested struct TWO
bytes wide was never affected, which is why the family had three members
and not thirty.

What distinguishes the two is not a width: **it is whether the member
names a struct of this schema and is one of it**, which is the question
the branch asks now. The sixth branch in these increments keyed on a
shape a member usually has rather than on what the member is, after the
packed size field, the varint size field, the element-count ordering,
`_len` on a run measured in elements, and `situ_at_len`.

The composition is what the fix buys, and it is the ordinary one:
`situ_flags_build` writes the byte and `situ_header_build` takes it as
bytes, like every other nested member. `A8` is `1010 1000` -- urgent
set, ack clear, priority five, and the reserved three bits zero because
the schema says so -- and the header comes out
`01 02 A8 00 10 00 03 11 22 33 44` with the reader finding the bits
inside the byte again.

**And the message's only corpus instances were all three of those
misdiagnoses**, which is a new way for a claim to go quiet: the gate
reported the row unemitted the moment the fault was fixed. What would
still reach it is `u8 x[]` with nothing stating its length, and the
parser refuses that outright -- *an array needs a size here* -- so it is
listed as constructed, a net for a shape nobody has found, like the
reserved fall-through 26.628 left in the same position.

**179 of 242 structs build**, 36 of 45 schemas, 96 of 112 arms.

#### What is left is mostly correct refusals

80 refusals in 35 families before this, 77 after, and the top of the
list is things a writer at this rung SHOULD decline: nine sealed
regions, whose interior is written through the seal and needs a key that
is rung 3's; eight tags whose schema names no codec, which situ cannot
invent; seven coded regions, where the bytes are a codec's output; five
registers, which are bus transactions rather than bytes in a buffer.

Of the rest, one is a decision rather than a gap and belongs to the
copyright holder: **four structs are refused as "entirely literal, so
there is nothing to build"** -- json's `true`, `false` and `null` among
them. The refusal is accurate and the rule behind it was deliberate:
`_encode` of a constant is not a builder. But an adopter composing a
JSON document then hand-writes those four bytes, which is the
duplication this compiler exists to remove, and situ emits no constant
for them to use either. Whether a struct with nothing for a caller to
supply should get a builder is a question about what a builder IS, so it
is recorded here rather than answered in passing.

### 26.632 Escaping is forced, not invented -- and three copies of one cap

Three refusals said a run *"escapes its delimiter, and escaping would
write bytes other than the ones it was given"*. That is true and it is
not a reason. **The caller hands over CONTENT and the wire form is the
schema's**, which is the division every other member here already
follows: a size field is computed, a pad is computed, a checksum is
computed, and these bytes are encoded.

What makes it not an invention is that the encoding is **forced**.
`situ_scan_relaxed` takes the byte after an escape as content whatever it
is, so exactly two kinds of byte must carry one:

  - the delimiter, or the run reads back shorter than it was written;
  - the escape byte itself, or it swallows the byte after it -- and a
    content byte ending in one swallows the DELIMITER, leaving the member
    unterminated, which is the fault `sexpr`'s own comment describes from
    the reading side.

**Nothing else is escaped**, and that is the line: a JSON encoder also
escapes control bytes, and situ's `[escape = ...]` does not say so. It
says which byte escapes, and the reader accepts any byte after it.

So json's and sexpr's strings and `edges.escaped_run` build:
`a"b` comes out `"a\"b"`, `ab\` comes out `"ab\\"`, and the reader's own
scan finds its delimiter in both.

**The sabotage separates the two rules, and only one of them is caught by
`_validate`.** Dropping the escape-the-escape rule makes `ab\` fail the
build -- the closing quote is escaped, the member is unterminated, and
the struct's own validation refuses it. But `a\b` comes out `"a\b"`,
which the reader accepts **at the same length** while meaning something
else under the escape rule: `\b` is one escaped byte rather than two
content ones. That half is invisible to every check situ has, which is
the argument for the rule rather than for the validation, and the reason
the test asserts bytes.

#### The cap was three copies of one rule, all short by one

`[max = N]` bounds the member's bytes, and the reader's scan window is
`min(N, remaining)` -- so the delimiter has to land INSIDE the cap and
the rule is "content and delimiter together". **This writer checked it in
three places and every one read it as "content"**: a delimited run, an
escaped run, and minimal digits. Each accepted exactly one length that
`_validate` then refused.

Measured, with `max 8` and `max 4`: seven content bytes build and eight
return CONSTRAINT having agreed to them; three digits build and four do
the same. A builder that reports CONSTRAINT for an input it accepted at
plan time is the honest-but-useless state a refusal by name exists to
avoid, and here it was produced by arithmetic rather than by a missing
branch.

**They are gone rather than corrected**, which is 26.628's answer to a
pad's bounds and is this file's own stated rule: two checks of one schema
is how they come to disagree, and these had. The view states the cap, the
builder validates against the view before returning, and that catches
every over-cap run by construction -- an over-long run is precisely one
whose delimiter is not in the window. Behaviour measured identical with
the checks in and out, at the boundary and either side of it.

What the cap means is now visible in the escaped case:
`edges.escaped_run` is `until "," max 64 [escape]`, so a comma in the
content costs two of the sixty-four, and 62 bytes with one in them take
the same budget as 63 without. That is the one place the three-way
relationship -- content, encoding, cap -- can be seen at all, which is
why the test is written over it.

#### Two more things the loop had to get right

The length is accumulated **against the room left** rather than summed
and compared afterwards: a content length near `UINT32_MAX` doubles past
it, and a wrapped total passes a capacity check it should fail.
`situ_cap - situ_at - situ_need` cannot wrap, because the running total
is at most the capacity by induction.

And the null check goes **before** the loops rather than inside the copy,
unlike every other caller-measured run here: those skip a `memcpy` at
zero length, where these loops read bytes one at a time. A length with a
null pointer is the caller's mistake and it gets BOUNDS, not a crash.

**176 of 242 structs build**, 36 of 45 schemas, 96 of 112 arms.

### 26.631 Two writing primitives the runtime did not have

Seven refusals were one family: the runtime could not write the bytes.
Four were big-endian base-128 varints -- SQLite's record varints, and
three in `edges` -- and three were text numbers the schema declares
signed. Both are runtime gaps rather than generator ones, which is the
distinction that decides where the fix goes: a second implementation in
the generator is the fault `owned.py` paid for in BCD, where an encode
and a decode were self-consistent and wrong together.

**`situ_varint_be_put` is the decoder backwards, beside it.** The runtime
had `situ_varint_be_get` and `situ_varint_be_len` and no encoder, so the
length comes from that same `_len` -- the function the minimality check
reads -- rather than from arithmetic done twice. SQLite's ninth byte is
the case worth stating: `terminal_bits == 8` means it carries all eight
of its bits and ends the value whatever its high bit says, which the
decoder does unconditionally at `max_bytes - 1`, so the encoder must too.
A value too wide is refused rather than truncated, because `_len` clamps
its answer to `max_bytes` and the write would otherwise drop the high
bits silently.

Round-tripped at every boundary against the decoder, which is the only
check that catches a sign or shift error: 0, 127, 128, 2^14-1, 2^56-1,
2^56 and UINT64_MAX through SQLite's nine-byte form, and MIDI's
four-byte one beside it. 2^56 comes out `80 C0 80 80 80 80 80 80 00`, and
a cell with a 200-byte payload writes its size as `81 48` and a rowid of
300 as `82 2C` -- SQLite's own spelling.

**`situ_format_int` is `situ_parse_int` backwards**: `-` and never `+`,
no `-0`, and `len` is the whole field including the sign, as
`situ_format_uint`'s is including its leading zeros. The magnitude is
`-(value + 1) + 1` rather than `-value`, which is undefined at
INT64_MIN -- and INT16_MIN is in the test for the same reason, since a
writer that negates the value rather than its predecessor is wrong at
exactly one input.

For `[minimal]` the sign is a byte of width on top of the magnitude's
digits, counted in the generated code because that is where the digit
count already lives. All six values round-trip through the reader's own
getter and `_validate`.

#### A varint can be the size field, and that is three for three

`payload_size` was in the signature. SQLite's cell is
`payload_size`, `rowid`, `payload[payload_size]`, so the caller was
passing the size AND the payload's length -- two numbers for one fact,
with nothing to stop a message disagreeing with itself.

**The third branch in two days to take a value for a member the schema
says the writer computes.** A packed field was the first (26.630), a
varint the second, and the element-count branch ordering was the third.
The cause is structural and worth stating where the next branch will be
written: the size-field check sits AFTER every branch keyed on what a
member IS, so each of those branches has to ask the question itself or
silently win. Three instances is a pattern rather than three bugs.

`VARINT` was also missing from `CALLER_SUPPLIED`, which came out when the
signature guard dropped every varint rather than the computed one: a
struct whose only caller-supplied member is a varint would have been
reported as "entirely literal, so there is nothing to build".

#### The guard that had to arrive with the signed support

`_radix_refusal` returns before `_scalar_refusal`'s own `scaled` check,
so a `scaled i64` written in digits was being refused for its SIGN.
Handle the sign and it falls through to a writer that formats an
integer: **1.5 written as 1**, which is `f32 x[2]` from the previous day
in a second construct. The scaled check now lives in the radix table
where it is reachable, and json's numbers and edges' `measured` say what
is actually in the way.

That is twice now that adding a capability would have un-refused
something that needed a different refusal. The habit that catches it is
reading the branch ORDER rather than the branch: a refusal table ordered
by what a member lacks answers for whatever it reaches first.

#### An out-parameter read in its own call, for the fourth time

`printf("%d %llu", f(view, &size), size)` prints the value `size` had
before the call, because the arguments are unsequenced. It has now
happened four times in these increments, every time in a throwaway C
probe, and every time the symptom was a plausible wrong number rather
than a crash -- here `0 0` for a writer that was correct.

The rule is in the probes as a comment now, where the next one gets
written: **call it, then print it.** A probe is not a test and gets
written fast, which is exactly why the same hazard keeps finding it.

#### Three tests pinned refusals this removed, and one had moved twice

`test_a_nested_struct_whose_extent_its_bytes_do_not_state_is_refused`
asserted a misdiagnosis for a day, was corrected to pin the LEB128-only
refusal, and that is gone as well. A message pinned twice is a message
the test should not be pinning, so it checks the property underneath --
a varint type has no `_required`, read from the artifact -- and that the
planner reaches its varint branch at all.

The BE128 refusal test became a statement about which encoder the writer
calls and that it passes the declaration's own `max_bytes` and
`terminal_bits`, the same properties `emit.py` hands the reader. And the
signed digits case left the refusal table for a test that asserts bytes.

**173 of 242 structs build**, 36 of 45 schemas, 96 of 112 arms.

### 26.630 Running a size expression backwards, and the canonical IPv4 header

The largest family left was ten refusals saying *`X` is sized by the
expression `E`, which this writer cannot invert* -- and it could invert
eight of them. A reader is handed a field and derives a length; a writer
is handed a length and has to derive the field, which for `length - 8`
is `payload_len + 8` and for `(ihl - 5) * 4` is `options_len / 4 + 5`.

**The boundary is affine in exactly one field with a positive scale**, and
it lives in `invariant.py` rather than in the C writer, because which
expressions can be run backwards is a question about the schema and a
second writer would ask it the same way. `invariant.invertible` folds the
expression into `scale * field + offset` and `inversion_refusal` says
which operator or shape stopped it, from the same walk so the two cannot
disagree about a case. The corpus's own expressions are the test table:
eight invert, and the four that do not each name their obstacle -- floor
division, where two field values give one length; two fields, where one
length cannot say what both hold; ID3's synchsafe `|`; and the
`align_up(x, 4) - x` padding, whose whole point is that the result
depends on where the run lands rather than on how long it is.

**Exact or refused.** Three bytes of IPv4 options are a length no `ihl`
can state, and the writer answers CONSTRAINT: rounding up would write a
header claiming a length the bytes do not have, and rounding down would
hide an option byte from every reader.

#### The vector that needed both increments

    45 00 00 73 00 00 40 00 40 11 B8 61 C0 A8 00 01 C0 A8 00 C7

RFC 791's worked example, byte for byte, and **two of those bytes are not
given to the builder at all**. The low nibble of `45` is `ihl`, derived
from zero bytes of options; `B861` is the checksum, computed once the
message is whole. With either half missing the header has no builder, so
one twenty-byte vector exercises 26.629 and this entry together.

UDP is the same arithmetic in the other direction -- `length - 8` solving
to ten bytes for a two-byte payload -- and it comes out
`12345678000A3AC24869`, the checksum again being the hand-computed
`0x3AC2`.

#### A packed member can be the size field, which nothing had met

IPv4's `ihl` is four bits wide. The packed branch runs before the
size-field check, so `ihl` became a caller's parameter and the run after
it was told *"`options` has no stated length, so nothing says when the
writer should stop"* -- a true sentence about a schema that states it
exactly. A size field is the writer's to compute whatever its width, so
the packed branch asks `measures` first now and sets the bits from the
run.

**And that was already wrong for the simpler shape beside it.**
`edges.packed_driver` is `u4 n; u32 d[n]`, and the caller was passing
BOTH `n` and the run's count: two numbers for one fact, with nothing to
stop a message saying four elements and carrying five. It is computed
now, and the parameter is gone rather than ignored -- an unused one fails
the generated file's own `-Wunused-parameter`.

#### Found by diffing the set, not by counting it

That packed case was collateral: the first cut of the size-field check
refused a packed member whose run has no expression between them, so
`edges.packed_driver` lost its builder in the same pass that gained
seven. **The total went from 161 to 167 and the loss was invisible** --
six is what a net gain of seven minus one looks like, and nothing in the
numbers says which.

What found it was a second worktree at the previous commit, listing the
buildable structs by name in both and diffing. `evidence.md`'s *a count
inherits its detector* is about the instrument; this is the same hazard
one level up, where the instrument is fine and the SUMMARY is lossy. A
count cannot report a swap. So the measurement for an increment that
moves a set is the set.

It is 168 of 242 now, 36 of 45 schemas, 96 of 112 arms.

#### Elements, not bytes, where the run has them

`u16 a[n]` makes `n` a count of ELEMENTS -- the reader computes the byte
length as `n * 2` -- so an expression over such a run inverts in elements
too, and the arithmetic has to read the caller's `_count`. It read `_len`
first, which does not exist for a wide run, and the generated header did
not compile. Then the element-count branch matched ahead of the inverted
one and wrote the raw count: three elements where `n + 1` means the field
says two, with `situ_solved` computed and unused.

Both are the fault that produced `situ_at_len` this morning -- a name or
a branch chosen by the shape a member usually has -- and in both the
compiler was the detector, the second time through
`-Werror=unused-variable` on a value nothing read. Neither was reachable
from the corpus: `edges.wide_run` has `u16 a[n]` and `i32 b[n + 1]`
sharing one `n`, so it is refused for that instead, and the probe that
found both was an inline schema with one wide run.

#### The refusal had to move with it

`_member_refusal` was composing the reason from the expression alone,
which cannot see that the field it solves for is a struct argument, or
already measures something else. Asked about `edges.negotiated`'s
`trailer[block + 1]` it answered *"does not determine `block`"* about an
expression that determines it exactly -- while the real blocker was that
`block` is a struct argument (0050) and in none of the bytes this writer
puts down.

So the pass that wires an inversion now owns the reasons for the ones it
declines, and there are three: the field is not a member of this struct,
the field is a struct argument, or the field is already the stated size
of something else. `edges.arithmetic` is the third case nine times over
-- nine runs whose lengths are nine different functions of one `units` --
and the claim gate noticed the shuffle immediately, because *"comes from
a struct argument"* had lost its only corpus instance to a message that
was worse.

### 26.629 The internet checksums, and a refusal overturned by its own argument

Nine of the ninety-five refusals were *`X` covers `X`, which follows it,
so its value is not known when the writer reaches it* -- and the nine are
ICMP's checksum in six arms, IPv4's header checksum, TCP's and UDP's. The
most recognisable checksums in existence, and a message builder that
cannot write them is missing the obvious case.

**26.610 refused them deliberately, and the argument that overturns it is
in 26.610.** That entry says building needs no permission above rung 2
because *"appending into caller-supplied backing invalidates nothing: no
view into the buffer exists while it is being filled"* -- and then refuses
a tag inside its own coverage because it *"would need a back-patch"*. Both
cannot be true. If no view exists, nothing is invalidated by writing a
byte at offset ten either; the buffer is the writer's until it returns.

**And the writer was already filling tags out of order.** `_tags` takes
the field's address from the reader's own `_ptr`, computes with
`_compute`, stores, and proves the store with `_check`. It never asked
where the tag was -- so a trailing PNG CRC and a header checksum inside
its own coverage were one code path all along, and the only thing
stopping the second was a struct-level gate refusing to plan it.

**For these nine the reserved bytes are not even a placeholder.** RFC
1071 sums the message with the checksum field taken as zero, which is
what `[self_as = 0]` says in the schema and what the writer writes while
appending. The zeros are the thing itself.

So the rule split by **what is late**. A `located` member and an index
table are late POSITIONS: nothing learnt at the end repairs them, because
the bytes in between are already down. A tag is a late VALUE at a
position the schema fixes. `traverse.late_position_refusals` answers the
first question and is what the writer consults;
`traverse.tags_covering_later` answers the second and returns the pairs
rather than a flag, so a refusal built from it can say which member.
`append_only_refusals` is gone -- with the builder no longer asking it,
it had no caller and its message was emitted by nothing, which is a row
the claim gate would have carried for ever.

#### Proved against arithmetic from the RFC, not against situ

An echo request with type 8, code 0, identifier 0x1234 and sequence 1
builds as `0800E5CA12340001`. RFC 1071's sum over those bytes with the
checksum field zero is `0x0800 + 0x1234 + 0x0001 = 0x1A35`, whose
one's complement is `0xE5CA`. That number comes from the RFC's
arithmetic, so it is evidence about the bytes; the reader's own `_check`,
asserted beside it, is evidence that situ agrees with itself. Both are
worth having and they are not the same claim.

#### UDP's and TCP's refusal was false, and the arity said so

They were refused with *"is a tag whose schema names no codec"*. They
name one -- `internet_checksum` -- and the emitted `_compute` is right
there in the header. What differs is its **arity**: UDP's takes
`(view, prefix, prefix_len, out)` where ICMP's takes `(view, out)`,
because the sum runs over a twelve-byte pseudo-header that is nowhere in
the datagram. 14.2a's `prefix(...)` is the schema saying so.

The sixth misdiagnosis of this family, and the detector is the same one
that fixes it: `computes_itself` asked whether a *specific signature* was
in the header and reported its absence as "no codec". It asks both
signatures now, and `computes_over_a_prefix` is the separate question --
read from the artifact, because the header is what the call has to match.

**So the writer asks the caller for those twelve bytes**, and situ emits
a builder for the struct that holds them, so the two compose: build the
pseudo-header, hand it over, and this writer never has to know what an
address is. The length is checked against that struct's own `SIZE_FIXED`
macro, because it is the one thing a caller can get wrong silently -- a
short prefix sums to a different number and the message still validates.

Hand-computed again: pseudo-header words `0A00 0001 0A00 0002 0011 0008`
and message words `1234 0000 DEAD BEEF` sum with end-around carry to
`0xC3ED`, complement `0x3C12`, and the builder writes
`12343C12DEADBEEF`.

**The fixture for that is inline, and deliberately.** `udp_header` still
has no builder: `payload[length - 8]` needs an inverse this writer does
not have, and `ipv4_header` wants `(ihl - 5) * 4`. A test that waited for
them would have left the prefix path written and exercised by nothing,
which is the state this increment found `computes_itself` in.

#### What moved, and the two expectations that were wrong

ICMP's six arms build, so **161 of 242 structs and 96 of 112 arms** --
the arms are where this landed. IPv4, TCP and UDP now hit the next reason
along, which is the largest remaining family: ten refusals for a size
field the writer cannot derive from the run's length. `length - 8`,
`(ihl - 5) * 4`, `nla_len - 4`, `((hdr_ext_len + 1) * 8) - 2` -- affine
in one field, and invertible with a divisibility check. That is the next
increment, and it is what stands between this writer and the three most
familiar headers on the wire.

Two of my own tests had pinned the old behaviour and both were corrected
rather than updated: a parametrised case asserting `ipv4_header` is
refused for *"which follows it"*, and the claim-gate row for that
message. The first could not simply be repointed at the new reason --
without the header passed in, the tag is refused for having no
`_compute`, which stands in front of the refusal the case is about. So it
passes the header now, which is what `situc build` does and what the
test should have done from the start.

### 26.628 A reserved region has a content policy, and the writer ignored it

Four refusals said *`X` is reserved and has no stated length*, and the
four were three different shapes: an alignment pad, a length-hiding pad
with declared bounds, and a run sized by an expression. One message for
three facts is the 26.625 misdiagnosis class in the one place a caller
has nothing else to read -- and it was structural rather than careless.
The reserved branch in `plan` answered for every unsized reserved member
itself, ahead of `_member_refusal`, so the table's own `pad_to` and
`pad_bounds` entries were **unreachable**: two refusals written, never
emitted, and listed in the claim gate as constructed, which is how they
stayed green.

**And reading the policy found the worse half.** A reserved region was
written as zeros whatever the schema said, over a comment asserting
*"Zero is what a `must_be_zero` policy requires and what no other policy
refuses."* `must_be_one` refuses it. Measured by building one: a
`reserved u8 [must_be_one]` byte went down as `00`, the struct's own
`_validate` -- which this writer calls before returning -- rejected it,
and the builder answered `SITU_ERR_CONSTRAINT` for every input it could
ever be given. Accepted at plan time, useless at run time, which is the
state a refusal by name exists to avoid.

The corpus has two such members and both sit in structs refused for
unrelated reasons, so nothing here would have caught it. The fixture is
inline, and the test runs the builder rather than inspecting its plan:
the parts were right and the bytes were wrong, so a plan-level assertion
passes throughout.

**What the writer does now is one sentence: it writes the content the
schema states and takes the content the schema leaves open.**
`must_be_zero` and `must_be_one` are facts, so they need no caller --
`memset` of `0` or `0xFF`, and a packed group's reserved bits are set
rather than left in the zeroed group. `preserve` and `unknown` state
nothing, so the bytes come from the caller, which is 0032's closing
invariant reaching the one kind of member with no accessor to read it
back.

**The sub-byte half is the same rule one level down, and the corpus
cannot show it either.** A packed group is zeroed and each member set in
place, which IS the whole of `must_be_zero` -- so the other three
policies had to be said: ones are set from the schema, and `preserve`
and `unknown` bits come from a caller who gets a parameter for them
exactly as a field does, with the same refusal for a value too wide,
since `situ_bits_set_*` masks and a truncated value is a valid message
saying something else. The two `must_be_one` members in the corpus are 4
bits and 1 bit and both sit in refused structs, so the group path could
have written zeros over either and nothing here would have shown it.

`--owned` answers the same question by refusing such a struct, and the
difference is worth naming rather than looking like drift: an owned
struct holds fields rather than the buffer, so it has nowhere to keep
those bytes and cannot promise the round trip it exists for. A writer
has a caller who is holding them. Two mechanisms, each naming its own
reason -- the shape 0043's amendment used for the pad base.

#### The pad is the cursor, which 0043's amendment is what settles

`pad_to(n)` reaches the next n-byte boundary **from the base of the
struct that declares it**, not from the message base: 0043 said the
message base, and its 2026-09-04 amendment narrowed it, because a
struct's extent has to be a property of the struct or `SIZE_FIXED` is a
lie for every struct holding a pad. The writer's cursor is exactly that
offset -- it has written every member before the pad and nothing else --
so the length is computable with no caller and no analysis. Verified
against the reader rather than against itself: `_pad_offset` and
`_trailer_offset` are the reader's own arithmetic over the bytes that
came out, and every pad length from 0 to 3 puts the trailer where the
reader looks for it.

**The runtime gained `situ_pad_to_u32` for it, and the reason is that
the reader's helper is wrong here.** `situ_align_up_u32` saturates at
the view's limit, which is right for a reader -- an aligned offset past
a short frame is a truncated message for `validate` to report -- and in
a writer it silently SHORTENS the pad instead of refusing for want of
room. So the pad expression is its own function and `align_up` is that
function plus the clamp: one expression, two callers, and they cannot
disagree about where the next member starts.

**A runtime symbol has a second place to be named, and the gate knew
before I did.** `RUNTIME_SYMBOLS` in `codegen/c/names.py` is a literal
list of the runtime's definitions -- carried in situc rather than read
at generation time, because the header installs separately -- and it is
what stops a generated name colliding with a runtime one. Adding
`situ_pad_to_u32` to the header and not to the list failed
`test_the_runtime_symbols_are_the_runtime_s` an hour into `make check`,
which is the one-claim-two-places rule being enforced rather than
remembered. Nothing else lists them: the C++ reader, the dissector and
the walker all USE `situ_align_up_u32`, which is right, a reader wanting
the clamp.

**The control for that took two attempts, and the first one passed the
sabotage.** Asking `pickle_string` for a capacity too small for its pad
returns BOUNDS with the saturating helper too -- because the trailer has
no room either, so the right answer arrives for the wrong reason. With
the pad LAST there is nothing after it to run out of room and the two
separate: the clamp makes the pad zero bytes, the capacity check passes
over nothing, and the reader computing the same clamped arithmetic over
the same short buffer agrees the message is whole. Three bytes, reported
SITU_OK, where a peer reads four. That is the fifth guard in these
increments that the corpus fixture could not discriminate.

#### A length nobody measures is the caller's, in three spellings

`pad_random(min, max)` is 0045's construct, and that record settled it
as "a claim checked on parse" because situ writes readers and has no
random source. Writing one does not move that: the length is still the
sender's choice, so it is a parameter rather than something this
compiler invents, and what the schema states -- the bounds, the content
policy -- is what the writer holds to. Two more shapes turned out to be
the same part: a reserved run sized by a field, whose length nobody
measures because a reserved member has no accessor, and one that runs to
the end of the message, which 0045 names as the shape a schema could
already say without `pad_random`. Both had the wrong refusal too; the
field-sized one now has its size field computed from what the caller
passed, exactly as a byte run's is, so a message cannot disagree with
itself about how much padding it carries.

**The bounds are not checked by the writer, and that was measured rather
than assumed.** Removing the check left both ends of the range answering
CONSTRAINT exactly as before: the view states the bounds and this
builder validates against it before returning. Two checks of one schema
is how they come to disagree -- which the builder's own epilogue says,
and which a first cut had just violated.

#### The policy rule had six copies, in two conventions

`_reserved_policy` existed in `codegen/c/emit.py`, `codegen/c/owned.py`,
`codegen/c/checks.py`, and the C++, Python and Rust emitters. Four
return the policy name with `must_be_zero` as the default; `checks.py`
returns `str | None`, folding `preserve` and `unknown` into None because
it is answering what `validate` must CHECK rather than what the policy
IS -- a different question wearing the same name. The three C callers
read one definition in `traverse` now, which is where every decision of
this kind is answered once; the other three backends still hold their
own, and collapsing those changes generated output in three languages,
so it is its own piece of work rather than a side effect of this one.

**And one discrepancy left open rather than resolved.** 0043 says
`pad_to(n) [preserve]` "is the escape for a format that genuinely
carries data there"; the front end refuses the attribute in that
position -- *"`[preserve]` means nothing here: belongs on a `reserved`
member, whose policy it sets"*. One of them is wrong and which is a real
question: the parser's refusal makes every `pad_to` `must_be_zero`,
which is what let the writer's pad branch be total. Recorded for the
holder rather than settled from inside a writer increment.

**The writer now reaches 160 of 242 structs**, 36 of 45 schemas, 90 of
112 variant arms -- three more structs than 26.627, and two builders
that could not succeed for any input now can.

### 26.627 Elements wider than a byte, and asking what an element IS

Seventeen refusals named a run of elements that are not single bytes, and
they were two families rather than one. **Nine were arms holding a fixed
run of BYTES** -- writable with the role a struct's own byte run already
uses, and refused only because an arm's content had two cases and a run
was neither. **Eight were genuinely wider elements**: `u16`, `i16`,
`u32`, in `pickle` and `edges`.

**Elements are values, which the reader settles rather than this
writer.** `situ_edges_samples_get(view, index)` hands back a `uint16_t`
with the byte order applied, so the caller passes values and the byte
order is the writer's to apply -- not bytes already in wire order, which
would push the one job situ exists for back onto the caller.

**And the count is elements, measured rather than assumed.** For
`u16 a[n]` the reader computes `a_len` as `n * 2`, so `n` counts
elements; `pickle`'s `data[length]` is the same, `data_len = length * 2`.
So a size field measuring such a run states the count and the writer
multiplies -- where a byte run's size field is its length, because there
an element IS a byte.

A pickle wstring, hand-checkable against Python's own format:

    situ_pickle_wstring_build(out, cap, { 'h', 'i' }, 2, &n)
    -> 02 00 00 00 68 00 69 00

Length 2 as a little-endian `u32`, then `h` and `i` as little-endian
`u16`s. It reads back as two elements spelling `hi`.

**The probe that checked a refusal's reachability caught a fault I had
just written.** `f32 x[2]` BUILT, and the store is
`situ_put_be32((uint32_t)x[i])` -- a numeric conversion, so 1.5 would go
on the wire as 1 rather than as its bits. The branch keyed on
`element_bits in (16, 32, 64)` and never asked what the element was. It
asks `_scalar_refusal` of the element now, which is the same question a
single scalar answers, and floats, BCD, fixed point and scaled elements
are refused by name.

**That is the fifth instance of one habit and the first time the habit
caught itself.** Three dead branches (26.611, 26.615, 26.626) were
guards for shapes the parser already rejects, and the remedy recorded
each time was: try the schema. Here that remedy was followed -- to find
out whether the generic *"is a run of N-bit elements, not of bytes"*
message was still reachable -- and it answered two questions at once:
the message IS reachable, because the parser accepts `u24 x[4]` and the
runtime has no 24-bit store, and the float case was broken. **The habit
paid for itself the first time it was applied deliberately.**

Both now have tests with constructed schemas, which is what the refusal
gate's second half demanded: `"is a run of"` had gone quiet over the
corpus and could not be listed as constructed without something
reaching it.

Re-measured, same method -- the 45 schemas `every_schema` holds: **157 of
242 structs have a builder, in 36 of the 45 schemas**, with **90 of 112
variant arms** writable, and 104 refusals left. Of the six largest
remaining, five are things situ should not write at all: a sealed region
needs a key, eight tags name no codec, a coded region is the codec's
output, a tag covering what follows needs a back-patch, and a register is
not a buffer.

### 26.626 A `while` run is proved by the reader's own count, not by its predicate

The last large refusal was a run that repeats while a condition holds --
fourteen of them, every one a run of structs whose predicate reads a
field: `sep == ','`, `nla_len >= 4`, `kind == 0x11`.

**Reading the generated loop is what made it tractable.** The reader
tests the predicate AFTER each element:

    at = start
    while at < limit:
        size = <element>_extent(element at `at`)
        if size == 0 or at + size > limit: break
        at += size; n += 1
        if !(predicate of that element): break

So elements 1..N-1 must satisfy it or the reader stops early, and the run
then ends where the frame does. **A writer could evaluate that predicate
only by re-emitting the expression**, which is a second derivation of the
reader's own loop -- the fault this project keeps paying for.

**So the reader is asked instead.** The writer walks the caller's bytes
with the element's `_required`, counts the elements, and compares its
count with what the generated `_count` reports for the finished message.
Two independent measurements that must agree, and **it needs no knowledge
of what the predicate is**: a schema whose condition this writer could
never evaluate is written anyway. Same move as the checksum's `_check`
proving the store (26.622) and the element validate (26.620) -- ask the
artifact rather than reproduce its logic.

Measured: every one of the nine `while` runs in the corpus has a
generated `_count`, so the predicate's reach was never the obstacle.

**The control is the case where the reader stops early**, and the
trailing-comma case is in the test as the one that is NOT a
disagreement:

    items `1,2]`  ->  `[1,2]`, reader counts 2    built
    items `1,2,`  ->  `[1,2,`, reader counts 2    built, and correctly:
                                                  the run ends at the frame
    items `1]2]`  ->  refused: the reader stops after the first element
                      and the second is bytes nobody reads

With the count comparison removed the last one builds and `_count`
reports 1. Whether `[1,2,` ought to be legal is `json.situ`'s business,
not the writer's, and the test says so to stop anybody tightening it
here.

**Two faults of mine on the way, and the second is the third instance of
one habit.**

A flag meant "the walk keeps a count" and was read as "there is a
declared count to compare", so every `while` run was asserted to have
exactly **zero** elements and all of them refused. One flag, two
questions.

And I wrote a refusal saying a run of BYTES has no element boundary for a
count to check -- true, and **unreachable**: the parser refuses
`u8 x[] while (...)` with *"`x` repeats `u8`, which is not a struct"*.
The branch is gone and the test asserts the parser's refusal in its
place. **Third time a guard here was written for a shape the front end
already rejects**, after 26.611's zero-delimiter minimal run and
26.615's zero-delimiter struct run, and the remedy is the same each time
and is one command: try the schema before writing the branch.

Both were caught by the refusal gate's second test (26.625) rather than
by the suite: no `while` message was emitted anywhere in the corpus, and
the gate requires every claim in its table to be emitted or listed as
constructed. **A row going quiet is how a branch announces it is dead.**

Re-measured, same method -- the 45 schemas `every_schema` holds: **150 of
242 structs have a builder, in 35 of the 45 schemas**, up nine structs
and one schema, and 118 refusals remain. What leads them now is a sealed
region (9), the eight tags naming no codec, a coded region (7), a tag
covering what follows it (6), a run of 16-bit elements (6) and a register
(5) -- and four of those six are things situ should not write at all.

### 26.625 Every refusal carries a claim, and the gate catches the half that is false

Five of the builder's increments produced a message right in VERDICT and
wrong in REASON, and twice a test of mine had pinned the wrong message in
place so that correcting it would have gone red. A refusal is the
builder's only interface for everything it cannot do, and it was the
least-checked thing in it. So the messages were audited and the audit was
made a gate.

**The census first: 32 distinct messages over 132 refusals**, from 30
refusal sites. Three families were wrong or useless:

  - **18 of the 132 came from one fallback**, `f"is a {kind}"` --
    *"is a sealed"*, which is not a sentence, and the same for `coded`,
    `tlv` and `marker`. A kind as the whole reason. Each has one now: a
    sealed region needs a key, which is rung 3's; a coded region puts the
    codec's output on the wire and not what a caller hands over; a TLV
    region's present fields are a choice no parameter here expresses --
    the gap a variant had before 26.617; a marker's value the schema
    pins, and a pinned SCALAR takes a different path from a pinned run.
  - **17 hedged between two reasons the code could tell apart**: *"either
    its own bytes do not state its extent, or it ends `before` a byte it
    does not own"*. Measured: **fifteen were the first and two the
    second**, and both facts are in hand at the refusal. They say which
    now.
  - **7 of those 17 named a `u8`** -- arms holding a byte RUN, told a
    message about structs. An arm's content is one member and it is
    whatever that member is.

**The gate found a fifth misdiagnosis on its first run.** `native.wide`
is a `u24` at offset 0: whole bytes, sharing nothing with anybody, and it
was being told *"it shares a byte with its neighbours"*. Two reasons were
one message -- a sub-byte field shares a byte, and a u24 occupies three
of them and has no store -- and the second says so now: *"whole bytes and
not a width the runtime stores -- 8, 16, 32 and 64 are"*.

**What the gate is.** Each message carries a claim about the member, as a
predicate, and the claim is asserted against the member the message
names, over all 45 schemas. It also holds two shapes no single message
owns: every member-level refusal names its member first -- the only ones
that name none are the three about the struct -- and every claim in the
table is either emitted over the corpus or listed as constructed, so the
table cannot accumulate rows for messages that were reworded away.

**And it catches two of the five, which is the honest number.** A
claim-check catches a message whose claim is FALSE of the member:
reinstating the varint-as-nested-struct and the u24-shares-a-byte faults
turns it red. It cannot catch a claim that is TRUE and beside the point,
and both of the remaining faults were that:

    symbol.name     3 delimiters, told "ends at any of 3 delimiters"
    will_message.topic   element_bits None, told "is a run of 0-bit elements"

Each claim held. What was wrong was that the property named was not the
one that decided the refusal, and no predicate over one member can say
which branch should have fired. **So the gate is a floor on the
messages, not a proof of them** -- it removes the half that is checkable
and leaves the half that needs the author to have ordered the branches by
what a member IS.

One row went quiet in a way worth keeping: *"bits wide, so it shares a
byte"* HAD a corpus population and lost it, because every sub-byte member
in the corpus is now written as part of a packed group (26.618). The only
routes left are an arm holding a sub-byte scalar and a sub-byte size
field, and the corpus has neither -- so the table's second test is what
noticed, which is the stale-claim class caught by a gate rather than by a
sweep.

### 26.624 `\r\n` is one delimiter, and the control I wrote first tested the bound

Eleven members ended at a multi-byte delimiter and every one was a
single, consumed, two-byte sequence -- `\r\n` in http, smtp and edges,
`: ` in one. So there was nothing to decide: the single-byte and
multi-byte forms are **one emitter**, because the one-byte case is the
other with N = 1, and a second comparison written for it is a second
thing to be wrong.

Three sites use it: the scan that refuses a byte run containing its own
delimiter, the boundary check in a struct run, and the write. All three
now take the sequence.

**A real HTTP request head builds, every byte from generated code:**

    GET / HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: example.invalid\r\n\r\n

41 bytes -- the line from `request_line_build`, the field handed over as
bytes because a `header_field` ends at TWO delimiters and is refused for
that, and **the blank line written by the run's own delimiter**. It
acquires a view.

**The control I wrote first tested the loop bound rather than the
comparison**, and that is the part worth keeping. A sequence scan must
accept a CR *not* followed by LF, since that is not the delimiter -- so
the fixture is a version carrying one. My first was `HTTP/1.1\r`, with
the CR last, and it passed with the needle cut to its first byte:
`scan + 2 <= len` never reaches the final byte, so the bound excluded it
either way. The fixture that discriminates is `HTTP\r1.1`, with the CR in
the middle where the scan looks: correct, it is accepted; first byte
only, it is refused.

That is `evidence.md`'s *a control has to be reached* for the fourth time
in two days, and the first three were upstream checks intercepting the
case. This one was intercepted by **the loop bound of the very check
under test** -- which is nearer to home and harder to see, because the
sabotage and the interception live in the same four lines.

**And a parametrized case was removed rather than reworded.** The table
of delimiters the writer cannot place had a `\r\n` row asserting the
refusal this entry deletes. There is no refusal left to assert, so the
row is gone; what remains is one ambiguity the schema has -- several
delimiters -- and two transformations of the caller's bytes, escaping and
trimming.

Re-measured, same method -- the 45 schemas `every_schema` holds: **141 of
242 structs have a builder, in 34 of the 45 schemas**, up eight structs
and two schemas. What leads the refusals now is a `while` run (14), a
sealed region (9), the eight tags naming no codec, a codec (7), and a
`u8` run whose length nothing states (7).

### 26.623 A varint, and the fourth time a branch ordered by absence misread a member

The largest refusal after the checksum named a construct that does not
exist: **fifteen refusals said "is a nested `remaining_length`"**, and
`remaining_length` is mqtt's varint type. A varint has no `scalar` and a
`type_name` naming no struct, so it fell through to the nested-struct
branch, which is reached by what a member LACKS.

**That is the fourth misdiagnosis of this family in two days** -- after
the `before` run told about its delimiter count (26.612), the nested
field called a run (26.614), and the arm parameter chopped out of a local
(26.617). Every one had a correct verdict and a reason about something
else, and every one came from a branch ordered by absence. The remedy
each time was to ask first what the member IS.

**And a test of mine was holding this one in place.** 26.614's test
asserted the refusal text *"nested `edge_varint`"* -- so the suite pinned
the misdiagnosis, including the wrong half, and would have gone red if
the message were corrected without the test. A test that pins a message
pins whatever the message says. It now checks the refusal that applies.

**Writing one needs no new arithmetic**: `situ_varint_put` encodes
minimally and returns the bytes written or zero, and `situ_varint_len` is
beside it. So the writer bounds the value by the schema's `max_bits`,
calls the runtime, and advances by what it reports. Against LEB128's own
vectors, with 321 being MQTT 2.2.3's worked example:

    0          -> 00
    127        -> 7F
    128        -> 8001
    321        -> C102
    268435455  -> FFFFFF7F
    268435456  -> SITU_ERR_CONSTRAINT

The last is the standard's *"the receiver MUST close the network
connection"* seen from the writing side: one past 28 bits is refused
rather than written in five bytes.

**Two of the corpus's four varint types stay refused**, and by name:
sqlite's and edges' are BE128, which has a reader and a length function
and **no encoder**. Writing one here would be a second implementation of
a conversion whose first lives in the runtime -- `owned.py`'s BCD, where
an encode and a decode were self-consistent and wrong together.

**The parameter the writer needed was the fourth, so the four became
one.** `plan` had grown `header`, `prefix`, `structs` and `arm`, and the
varint declarations would have made a sixth positional argument. They are
a `Shape` now, and what makes it more than tidiness is that every field
is read from something the compilation already produced -- the emitted
header for `_required` and `_compute`, the resolved schema for a nested
type, the declarations for an encoding -- rather than derived a second
way. An absent field means the writer refuses more rather than guesses,
which is the direction 26.614 established.

Re-measured, same method -- the 45 schemas `every_schema` holds: **133 of
242 structs have a builder, in 32 of the 45 schemas.** Only one more
struct than before, which is the honest result: the fifteen refusals were
fifteen ARMS of one struct, and fixing what they said revealed the next
real reason in fourteen of them. What leads now is a `while` run (14), a
multi-byte delimiter (10), a sealed region (9), the eight tags naming no
codec, and a codec (7).

### 26.622 A trailing checksum, computed where the caller has the whole message

PNG's chunk builds, CRC and all, and the proof is a vector situ did not
produce:

    0000000049454E44AE426082

That is the IEND chunk every PNG file ends with -- length 0, `IEND`, and
the `AE426082` the specification states. The second case is checked
against `zlib` in the test rather than against situ's own recompute, for
the reason `evidence.md` gives: a round trip through `_check` says the
writer agrees with itself, and a vector from the format says it agrees
with PNG.

**`validate` deliberately does not verify a checksum**, and the generated
header says why: *"the coverage may run to the end of the message, and a
constraint walk that costs a file read is not the flat model 0051 settled
on. Call it where the caller has the whole message."* **The writer is
that caller** -- which is 26.620's argument arriving at a second
construct, two days' worth of findings apart in the same session. So the
tag's bytes are reserved where the writer reaches them, zeroed, and
filled after the view is acquired.

**Only three of the twelve refused tags could be done, and the predicate
is read from the artifact.** Nine name no codec -- a MAC, a signature --
so no `_compute` is emitted and situ cannot invent one; `computes_itself`
asks the header for the declaration, as `frames_itself` does. The three
are PNG's CRC at 32 bits and two 16-bit sums.

**Which check earns its keep differs by width, measured rather than
assumed.** Flipping the emitter's byte order turns the PNG test red --
the byte vector catches it -- while deleting the generated `_check`
leaves it green, so for PNG the vector is the guard and `_check` is
redundant. For the 16-bit sum there is no external constant, and with the
order flipped that case comes back `SITU_ERR_CHECKSUM` **from `_check`**:
capable rather than merely present, which is the one thing a guard with
no test of its own needs to show. Both widths now assert bytes, so each
has a guard that does not depend on the other.

**And a test that asserted a refusal had to be restated rather than
updated.** 26.610's trailing-tag case existed to show that
`append_only_refusals` does not refuse a tag that comes after what it
covers, and it demonstrated that by checking the struct was refused for a
*different* reason -- that nothing computed a checksum. That reason is
gone, so the test now asserts the stronger form: the struct builds, and a
`TAG` part is in its plan. Sabotaging the positional check still turns it
red while the three genuine append-only refusals stay green, so the
discrimination survived the rewrite.

Re-measured, same method -- the 45 schemas `every_schema` holds: **132 of
242 structs have a builder, in 32 of the 45 schemas**. What leads the
refusals now is a nested `remaining_length` (15), a `while` run (14), a
multi-byte delimiter (10), a sealed region (9) and the eight tags with no
codec, which are not situ's to compute at all.

### 26.621 The cut has no outlier to lead with, and that decides how it can be done

26.608 measured this document at 88 per cent log and called that the
number to act on. The holder's instruction was to cut it: keep each
entry's rule and its load-bearing number, drop the narration, **one
commit per pass rather than by attrition** -- the shape `evidence.md`
took on 2026-09-04, from 3044 lines to 1989.

**Measured before starting, and the measurement says the pass cannot be
done the way the instruction asks.** 620 entries, 38,974 lines between
them, **mean 62 and median 55**, longest 543:

    top  50 entries     7,194 lines   18% of the entry text
    top 100 entries    11,779 lines   30%
    top 200 entries    19,099 lines   49%
    top 400 entries    30,465 lines   78%

So there is no fat tail. Cutting the fifty longest entries perfectly
removes under a fifth of the text, and reaching three quarters of it
means touching **four hundred entries**, each wanting a judgement about
which of its numbers is load-bearing. That is not one session's work,
and it is work whose quality depends on having written the entry: of the
620, this session wrote eleven.

**A twenty-entry nibble is the thing the instruction rules out**, and for
a reason this document can check: `git log -S` on a rule's own words
recovers the case from the commit that removed it, which works only while
the removals are deliberate commits rather than a trickle nobody can
name. So the choice is a real pass or none, and a real pass is a
different piece of work from the one that was authorised.

**And the measurement went wrong twice in the same way first**, which is
worth more than the figures. Both earlier attempts charged
`### Invariants to hold across all phases` -- 1,391 lines of standing
rules, the most load-bearing prose in the file -- to the entry above it,
reporting a 1,432-line `26.115` whose real length is 41. An entry's span
ends at the next heading of ANY depth, not at the next entry heading,
and a document with non-entry blocks inside its log section breaks the
simpler rule silently. **Twice, after the first correction was recorded**
-- so the record of a measurement error is not a guard against repeating
it, and the figures above are the first ones taken with the invariants
block excluded.

**What is left is a structural option, and it is not this session's to
take.** Section 26 is 84 per cent of the file, and its entries are cited
by number from everywhere -- which is exactly the justification
`CLAUDE.md` gives `doc/decision/`: a single file cannot give a stable
anchor per record, and a record that gets referenced needs one. Moving
the log out of `project.md` would leave the design document readable in
one window without any editorial judgement being spent, and it would
cost a rewrite of every path that reads `project.md` -- the docs gate,
the dangling-citation test, the conventions test -- plus a convention
other projects would then look at. **The option, its cost, and whose it
is: the copyright holder's**, per *Describing a thing thoroughly is a way
of proposing it*.

Until then the cut stays authorised and undone, and this entry is what a
session picking it up should read first, so that the measurement is not
taken a fourth time.

### 26.620 Measuring an element is not validating it

hull's finding 17: `_list_build` returned `SITU_OK` for elements the
schema refuses -- a non-minimal length against `[minimal]`, a space
canonical form has none of, and **an element never closed, so the list
was not either**. Reproduced here on a two-field element with
`[max = 3]`: `n = 9` measures like any other element, its own `_validate`
says `SITU_ERR_CONSTRAINT`, and the build said OK.

**The division is the reader's and it is deliberate.** A run's elements
are not validated by the struct that holds them -- *"an array's elements
are validated by the caller that chooses to walk them"* -- which is
hull's own finding 3 from the other side. What was wrong is that **the
writer IS that caller**: the walk is the thing choosing to walk them, so
validating each element is this design being followed rather than
contradicted. The element's own verdict is returned rather than a flat
CONSTRAINT, so a caller learns which failure it was.

**A single nested field was already covered**, which is worth recording
because it stops the next reader widening the fix: a nested struct's
members are part of the enclosing struct's entries, so the final
`_validate` does reach them. Measured, with the same constrained element
nested rather than repeated: refused before this change. Only the run
had the gap.

**The element's view spans the rest of the run, not its own measured
length.** The first attempt gave each element a view of exactly `need`
bytes and sexpr's `a ` came back `SITU_ERR_BOUNDS`: a `before` run cannot
be read from its own extent, because the byte that ends it belongs to
what follows -- 26.617's lesson arriving in a third place. The reader
walks elements with the rest still visible, so the writer's view does
too.

**And it closed a second hole nobody had asked about.** With every
element validated, a caller can no longer build a list whose items read
back with an element they did not intend: `a b ` -- a trailing space --
is now refused, because that space is hull's finding 1, the phantom
element, and the phantom does not validate. `a b` builds `(a b)` and
reads back as **two** items. So the write side now refuses what the read
side merely mis-counts, which is a stronger guarantee than the reader
gives alone, and the test asserts both halves rather than the phantom
count it asserted before.

**Seventeen findings from one adopter, and the split is worth reading.**
Fifteen were faults situ already had, one (26.619) was a regression situ
introduced, and this one is a gap that only existed because the builder
exists -- so it could not have been found before today. Five of the
seventeen came from reading situ's generated output or its emitters
rather than from using it.

### 26.619 The peek minimum counted peeks the data may never reach

**A regression I shipped in 26.616 and an adopter found at head.** The
fix that raised a struct's minimum to a static peek's end counted *every*
placement, and `layout.placements` carries a variant arm's interior and a
run element's under a dotted path. So:

    struct t { peek u8 k; variant v switch (k) {
                 case 1: big b;      /* big is 40 bytes then a peek */
                 default: small s; } }

    map said  size=41   where it had said  1..41
    the one-byte message `02`, which takes the OTHER arm -> refused

and a `peek u32` inside a run's element made `r { u8 o; e items[] until
")"; }` need five bytes, so the empty `()` was refused where two bytes
are a complete `r`.

**The fix is `traverse.is_own_member`'s rule** -- no dot in the name
below this struct -- written out in `layout.py` rather than imported,
because `traverse` is built on that module. A peek inside an arm is read
only when the data takes that arm, and a run of no elements reads no
element's bytes; neither is the enclosing struct's to require. `big`'s
own minimum is still 41, which is the half of 26.616 that was right.

**What the regression says about 26.616's own evidence is the part worth
keeping.** That entry recorded, correctly, that the corpus has three
peeked members -- one at offset 0 and two with dynamic offsets -- and
that **no corpus struct changes**. Both halves were true and together
they were the problem: a change that moves nothing in the corpus is a
change the corpus cannot judge, and I wrote that down as reassurance
rather than as the gap it was. The test I added carried its own schema
because of it, and carried only the case the fix was *for*.

So the lesson is not "add more fixtures" but which fixture was missing:
**the one where the thing being counted should not count.** I had a
